result.summary: Pausanias walks through the sacred precinct of Altis at Olympia, listing the many altars, the Hall of Leonidas and the Town Hall. He then describes the monthly sacrifices of the people of Elis, their ritual customs and their libations to foreign gods such as Ammon.

scenes.title: Approaches and altars of Altis
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes Phidias' workshop, the Hall of Leonidas, the olive tree for victors' crowns and the altars near them.

scenes.title: Altars at the horse start
scenes.summary: He lists altars near the horses' starting place, the Rostrum and the processional road, and gives opinions on the names Thermius and Coccoca.

scenes.title: Town Hall and monthly sacrifices
scenes.summary: He describes the Town Hall hearth and the monthly rites of the people of Elis, including libations to Ammon and heroes, and the banqueting-hall for victors.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias withholds sacred words and hymns, showing religious reticence.

analysis.text: The catalogue of altars shows how thoroughly cult shaped Olympia, with gods tied to horses, markets and fate.
Elis' ties to the oracle of Ammon show Greek religion's links with Libya, and the Roman governors' use of the Hall shows Roman rule.

fun_facts.text: Phidias' workshop at Olympia was excavated in the 1950s, and a cup inscribed with his name was found there.

language_notes.text: Altis is the sacred precinct of Olympia, enclosing the temples and altars; the workshop lay just outside its boundary.
"Bylanes" means narrow side streets or lanes; Pausanias glosses a local Elean word by its Athenian equivalent.
"The olive beautiful for its crowns" translates a cult epithet (Kallistephanos); the tree's name refers to the victors' wreaths made from it.
Pausanias refers ahead to his Arcadia book (Book 8), where he explains the goddess called Mistress (Despoina).
The Seat of Honour (Proedria) was the place reserved for the judges or officials presiding at the games.
"Where the horses start" refers to the hippodrome's starting place at Olympia, with its starting gates; the altar stands on the approach to it.
The Fates (Moirae) were goddesses of destiny; Zeus as "Decider of Fate" (Moiragetes) was thought to know and direct what they assign.
"Patron of Horses" renders the cult title Hippios, with Hippia as its feminine form, for deities protecting horses and chariot racing.
Acmenæ, apparently from Greek akmē, "prime" or "peak"; the title may mean Nymphs of vigor, but the translation does not explain it.
Agnaptus means "unfulled" or "unwrought" in Greek; Pausanias says the portico took this name from its architect.
Pausanias compares the Elean dialect form Thermius with Attic Thesmius, "Law-loving"; this is his own guess, as he says.
Pausanias openly admits he could not discover the origin of Coccoca, a typical scholarly honesty in his work.
Altis is the sacred precinct of Olympia, enclosing the temples and altars; the Town Hall (Prytaneion) stood within it.
Débris here means the accumulated ashes and remains of burnt offerings, not rubbish; the hearth is built up from them.
The Mistresses (Despoinai) were goddesses honoured in Greek cult, often linked with Demeter and her daughter; wineless offerings suit such deities.
The Interpreter of Antiquities was an official who explained local ancient customs and sacred lore to visitors and worshippers.
Ammon was the Libyan god of the oracle in the desert, identified by Greeks with Zeus; Parammon is here said to be a title of Hermes.
Doric was the dialect of the Peloponnese and other regions; the hymns' dialect is noted as a mark of antiquity.

context_notes.text: Phidias was the great Athenian sculptor who made the gold-and-ivory statue of Zeus at Olympia; his workshop was used for that work.
Elis was the region and city that controlled Olympia and ran the games; under Roman rule its governors used the hall as their base.
The Seasons (Horae) were goddesses of the natural order and the year's cycle, often worshipped with Aphrodite.
Olympic victors received a simple wreath cut from this sacred wild olive, rather than money or valuable prizes.
Zeus and Artemis "of the Market-Place" (Agoraios, Agoraia) were worshipped as guardians of public gatherings and trade.
Castor and Pollux, the Dioscuri, twin sons of Leda, were patrons of horsemanship and athletes, which suits their altar near the course.
The Rostrum was the beak-shaped front of the starting structure at the hippodrome, resembling a ship's prow.
Altis was the sacred grove and precinct of Olympia, containing the main temples and altars.
Artemis of the Market-Place (Agoraia) was a cult title linking the goddess to civic life and the public square.
The great altar of Zeus at Olympia was said to be built up from ashes of sacrifices, mixed and moistened with water from the Alpheius.
Feasting victors at public expense in the town hall was a common Greek honour.

literary_notes.text: Addressing the reader as "you" and guiding by direction makes Pausanias a travelling guide walking the visitor through the site.
This brief aside shows Pausanias as a careful antiquarian, separating older official cults from recent private dedications.
Pausanias speaks in the first person as a careful investigator, offering a linguistic conjecture and signalling his own authority and its limits.
The candid admission of ignorance portrays the narrator as honest and unwilling to invent explanations.
The ever-burning hearth symbolizes the community's continuity and the unbroken link between the city and its gods.
Pausanias speaks as a cautious, pious witness, withholding sacred secrets and so signalling his reverence and authority as a traveller.
